topic: Grand finale: mobile system design & everything

questions.question: In a mobile system design interview you are asked to 'design Instagram Stories'. What should you do first?
options: Start writing the Compose UI for the story viewer so there is concrete code to discuss and refine
Draw the full backend architecture, with databases, queues and CDNs, before talking about the client
Clarify scope and requirements: core features, offline needs, scale, platforms and the constraints that matter most
Choose the client libraries (Retrofit, Coil, Room) and explain each one's internals in detail
questions.explanation: Interviewers look for structure: agree on what you are building and which non-functional requirements (latency, offline, data use, battery) drive the design. Jumping into backend boxes or library names before that often designs the wrong thing. Library choices come later, as justified decisions inside the client architecture.

questions.question: Feature flags or remote config let you turn off a misbehaving feature without a store release, which matters because a shipped mobile build cannot be rolled back instantly for users who already installed it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Unlike a web deploy, an app version lives on devices until users update, and review plus rollout take time. A server-controlled flag can disable a crashing feature for every version that checks it. Flags need safe defaults when the config cannot be fetched, and stale ones should be cleaned up.

questions.question: The backend adds a new value `"REFUNDED"` to the `status` enum in an order API. Two-year-old app versions start crashing while parsing order lists. What is the client-side fix for the future?
options: Store raw JSON strings in the client database and only parse them when a screen needs to show the value
Have the server check each app version and only add new enum values once every user has updated the app
Make every response field nullable on the client, so any change in the server schema can never cause a crash
Decode unknown enum values to an `UNKNOWN` fallback and ignore unknown fields, so old builds degrade instead of crashing
questions.explanation: Old app versions stay installed for years, so clients must be tolerant readers: unknown enum cases map to a fallback (e.g. a default in kotlinx.serialization or a custom Codable init) and unknown keys are ignored. Making everything nullable spreads null checks everywhere and does not fix enums. The server should still version carefully, but cannot wait for every user to update.

questions.question: You are shipping a risky rewrite of the checkout screen. Which release strategy limits the blast radius best?
options: Release to 100% of users at once so every crash report arrives quickly and can be fixed in a single hotfix
Staged rollout (Play) / phased release (App Store) with the feature behind a remote flag, watching crash and conversion metrics
Ship it as a separate app so that problems in the new checkout cannot affect the main app's ratings
Keep the release in internal testing until QA has covered every device model the app supports
questions.explanation: Staged and phased releases limit how many users get a new binary, and a flag lets you switch the feature off even for users who already have it. Monitoring crash-free sessions, ANRs and business metrics tells you when to pause. A full release maximises damage, and exhaustive QA across all devices is not realistic.

questions.question: You design checkout for an app used on unreliable networks. Which choices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Queue the payment in an outbox and charge automatically whenever the device next comes online, even hours later
Show 'payment succeeded' only after the server confirms, never optimistically
After an ambiguous failure such as a timeout, query the payment status from the server before offering a retry
Create one idempotency key per checkout attempt and reuse it on every retry of that attempt
On a timeout, retry immediately with a new idempotency key so the server treats it as a fresh request
questions.explanation: Money is where optimistic UI and blind retries become dangerous: the user must see the real outcome, and retries must be recognisable as repeats. A timeout may have succeeded, so you check status before retrying. A silent charge hours later surprises users with a stale intent, and a new key per retry is exactly how double charges happen.

questions.question: A coroutine launched in `viewModelScope` keeps running after the user leaves the screen and the ViewModel is cleared, so it is a good place for an upload that must finish.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `viewModelScope` is cancelled in `onCleared()`, so leaving the screen cancels the work, and process death kills it anyway. Work that must finish belongs in WorkManager (or a background URLSession / BGTaskScheduler on iOS). A ViewModel can enqueue the work and observe its progress.

questions.question: A trading app shows 200 symbols, each updating about 10 times a second over a WebSocket. The list stutters. What is the best client design?
options: Keep the latest price per symbol in memory, subscribe only to visible symbols, and push UI updates at most about once per frame
Send price ticks through FCM / APNs instead of the socket so the system handles delivery and batching
Rebuild the whole list state on every tick so the UI is always exactly in sync with the latest messages
Write every tick to Room / Core Data and let the list observe the table, so it always matches the stored data
questions.explanation: The UI only needs the latest value per symbol at display rate, so conflating in memory and sampling per frame cuts work by orders of magnitude, and unsubscribing offscreen symbols cuts bandwidth. Writing 2,000 ticks a second to a database causes heavy I/O and endless query invalidations. Push is neither fast nor reliable enough for ticks.

questions.question: A search screen queries the network as the user types. Which Flow chain gives correct results without wasted work?
options: `query.debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged().flatMapMerge { repo.search(it) }`
`query.distinctUntilChanged().flatMapConcat { repo.search(it) }.debounce(300)`
`query.debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }`
`query.onEach { viewModelScope.launch { _results.value = repo.search(it) } }`
questions.explanation: `flatMapLatest` cancels the search for the old query as soon as a new one arrives, so a slow, outdated response can never overwrite newer results. `flatMapMerge` runs searches concurrently and shows whichever finishes last, which may be stale. `flatMapConcat` queues every query, and launching a coroutine per keystroke has the same race as merge.

questions.question: You are designing automatic photo backup (like Google Photos or iCloud Photos). Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Load the whole photo library into an in-memory list at startup so the upload queue is quick to scan
Upload originals over mobile data by default and without limits, so backups are never delayed
Detect new photos from MediaStore / PhotoKit change notifications and schedule constrained background work
Keep per-photo upload state in a local database so a restart continues where it stopped
Hash each file's content so duplicates and already-uploaded photos are skipped before uploading
questions.explanation: Content hashing avoids re-uploading the same bytes, a persisted per-item state makes the pipeline resumable, and OS change observers plus WorkManager / BGTaskScheduler handle new photos efficiently. Users usually expect Wi-Fi-only by default, or an explicit opt-in for mobile data. Libraries can hold tens of thousands of items, so the queue should be paged from the database, not loaded into memory.

questions.question: Android vitals flags excessive partial wake locks, and iOS energy logs show high background CPU. The app polls a REST endpoint every 60 seconds in the background. What is the best redesign?
options: Move the polling into a foreground service so the system treats the background work as legitimate
Replace polling with server push as a 'changed' signal, and do deferrable sync in WorkManager / BGTaskScheduler jobs with constraints
Use an exact alarm every 60 seconds on Android and a repeating Timer on iOS so polls happen on schedule
Keep the 60-second polling but shorten the wake lock timeout so each poll holds the CPU for less time
questions.explanation: Frequent polling keeps waking the radio and CPU, and each wake-up has a fixed cost far larger than the request itself. Push only wakes the app when something actually changed, and scheduled jobs let the OS batch work with other apps. Foreground services and exact alarms are for user-visible or time-critical needs and draw policy scrutiny, and an iOS Timer does not run while the app is suspended.
